tables.how: City payroll file, fiscal 2013 to 2026. Before fiscal 2017 the file gives each employee a number, and the rows under one number are added together; from fiscal 2017 it gives a name instead, and each payroll row is taken by itself, so that two people who share a name are never added together. Listed: every such record with regular salary of $40,000 or more and overtime at least equal to it: 2,041 rows, 379 of them in fiscal 2026 (376 different names within a department) and 29 in fiscal 2014. The case counts 351 for fiscal 2026 because its analysis adds together every payroll row that carries the same name in a year, whichever department it is in. That leaves out 25 of the fiscal 2026 rows here, where a namesake's salary is added in, and it counts once a name with two rows over the line. The last column says, row by row, whether the case's count includes it; 1 employee-years in the case's count across all years have no single row over the line and are not listed. The comparison: 35,636 payroll rows had a salary of $40,000 or more in fiscal 2026. Hours are on file from fiscal 2017; paid hours for each day divides them by 365.
tables.limits: Public employees’ names and pay are public record; nobody listed is accused of anything. Police and Sheriff vacancies rose sharply after 2020: covering mandatory posts with fewer people requires overtime, and the most senior staff get first call on it. Paid hours are not clock hours: they can include leave cashed out, standby pay and time credited at premium rates, and firefighters work 24-hour shifts, so their paid hours run far higher by design. A person who changed job class or retirement plan during a year has two payroll rows and can appear twice, or with only part of the year’s pay; the column of other rows shows what else the payroll prints under the name in that department. The count of years under one name and department is not confirmed to be one person. The file cannot show whether each hour was worked or whether a department kept to its own weekly caps; timekeeping records would.

tables.how: City payroll file: the overtime and salaries columns of every fiscal-year row, added up by the department code on the row, fiscal 2013 to 2026. Every department with pay in the year is listed, under the name the file gives it. Citywide, overtime was $174.6 million in fiscal 2014 (6.9% of salaries) and $513.4 million in fiscal 2026 (10.4%). Rows for fiscal 2026 come first, the largest first.
tables.limits: Some department codes changed between fiscal 2016 and 2017 (the water, power and wastewater enterprises became part of the Public Utilities Commission; Human Services, Emergency Management and the Board of Appeals were renamed), so a long series under one name can have a break. Fiscal 2026 holds 27 fortnightly pay periods in this file rather than 26, which lifts every amount for that year by about 4%. Overtime rises when posts are vacant and the work must still be covered; the table shows where it is paid, not whether it could have been avoided.
